rationale: B wins because it keeps the product story alive without pretending the missing proof is already in hand: "Glossier adds three fragrances as it pushes into 800 more Sephora doors" is a real beauty-trade lane. A is strong, but "Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" is the softer, profile-shaped substitute where the fragrance angle should have been. The difference is discipline: B turns the thin facts into testable reporting questions; A rejects one usable fact and keeps one comfy retrospective.
gaps_in_A: "Glossier launches three new fragrance products" — refusing this outright is too conservative. The first fragrance line extension launching alongside 800 more doors is a viable beauty-trade angle if framed with proof demands, not as naked product news.

"Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" — this is a soft company arc with no named founder, quote, or fresh conflict supplied. It risks becoming the contrarian DTC angle in a nicer jacket.

"The beauty brand born on a blog is coming to Kohl's" — this compresses Sephora at Kohl's into plain Kohl's. The contrast works only if the Kohl's door count is material; otherwise it is a clever headline looking for a spine.

"The prevailing belief is real: Glossier was built as the proof case for direct-to-consumer beauty" — plausible, but it imports market context the update did not prove. A reporter will want receipts, not folklore.
gaps_in_B: "in one step" — the facts say expanding from 600 to 1,400 doors, not that the rollout happens in one operational step. Small phrase, unnecessary overreach.
"Story type: customer-story" — the Sephora at Kohl's angle is retailer-format analysis, not a customer story. The label is sloppy even though the angle mostly works.
"so the launch date is the hook" — no exact launch date is supplied. The safe peg is that the products launch alongside the expansion, not a date you don't have.
